Nest
NEST
noun
From the Saxon nest, the bed or habitation a bird builds for her young; rendering the Hebrew qen, a nest or brood, and the Greek kataskenosis, a lodging-place, in the words of our Lord concerning the birds of the air.

Biblical Definition

The nest in Scripture is the small home a creature makes, and God takes notice of it. The law of Deu 22:6 forbids taking the mother bird with the young: “thou shalt not take the dam with the young” — a mercy statute so small that it proves the point of all the rest, that the God who governs empires legislates about a bird’s nest in a hedge. The psalmist, shut out from the courts of the LORD, envies the smallest tenant there: “Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts” (Psa 84:3). Even a sparrow has a place at those altars, and that is the ground of the pilgrim’s hope. Solomon warns of the man who leaves his post as “a bird that wandereth from her nest” (Pro 27:8), and the prophets turn the nest against the proud, telling Edom that though he set his nest among the stars he would be brought down (Oba 1:4). But the word gets its weight from our Lord: “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Mat 8:20). He who made every nest and numbered every sparrow was in this world without one. The homelessness is voluntary: He had no place to lay His head that His people might have a house not made with hands.

Webster 1828 Definition

The bed or habitation a bird builds for her young; guarded by God’s law, found even at His altars, and denied to the Son of man.

expand to see more

NEST, the place or bed formed by a bird for incubation and rearing her young.

From the Saxon nest; Hebrew qen; Greek kataskenosis, a lodging.

Protected by the mercy law of Deu 22:6, which spares the dam.

Figuratively, a man’s settled place, from which it is dangerous to wander (Pro 27:8).

Figuratively, a proud security thought unreachable (Oba 1:4; Jer 49:16).

Key Scripture

Deu 22:6 — "If a bird's nest chance to be before thee in the way in any tree, or on the ground, whether they be young ones, or eggs, and the dam sitting upon the young, or upon the eggs, thou shalt not take the dam with the young:"

Psa 84:3 — "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God."

Mat 8:20 — "And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head."

Pro 27:8 — "As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place."

Modern Corruption

Mat 8:20 is turned into a sentimental picture of a homeless teacher, and Deu 22:6 into a mere conservation rule — both stripped of the doctrine in them.

expand to see more

“The Son of man hath not where to lay his head” is quoted as pathos, a wistful line about a wandering teacher. It is nothing so soft. It is spoken to a scribe who had just volunteered to follow Him anywhere, and it is a demand that the man count the cost before he speaks again. And beneath the demand lies the deeper thing: the poverty is voluntary. He who fitted every hedge with a nest and clothed the lilies chose to own nothing, was born in a borrowed stable and buried in a borrowed tomb, and did it as the whole tenor of a life laid down. Take the pathos and leave the substitution, and the verse has been emptied.

Deu 22:6 suffers the opposite reduction, being filed away as an early conservation measure. It is a mercy statute, and its logic runs the other way: take the young if you have need, but do not take the mother with them — do not, in gratifying a present appetite, destroy the source of tomorrow’s provision, and do not harden yourself against the creature’s helplessness while she sits. Our Lord builds on exactly that scale when He says two sparrows are sold for a farthing and not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. The God who numbers the hairs of a man’s head is the God who wrote a law about a bird’s nest, and the smallness of the law is the size of the comfort.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The bird’s home — protected by law, found at God’s altars, denied to the Son of man.

expand to see more

Nest — Saxon nest; Hebrew qen; Greek kataskenosis, a lodging-place.

Deu 22:6: the dam is not to be taken with the young — a mercy statute of the smallest scale.

Psa 84:3: the sparrow and the swallow find a nest at the altars of the LORD of hosts.

Pro 27:8: the man who wanders from his place is a bird gone from her nest.

Mat 8:20: the birds have nests; the Son of man had nowhere to lay His head.

Usage

"God legislates about a bird’s nest — the smallness of the law is the size of the comfort."

"The sparrow has a place at His altars, and so may the pilgrim (Psa 84:3)."

"Mat 8:20 is not pathos; it is a bill handed to a volunteer before he enlists."
